data:
One Dark Factory instance is one Helm release: a control plane, a gateway and one PostgreSQL database, serving one tenant. Agents run in sandbox pods, one pod per run, in a namespace of their own. The rest of this page lists the components; Agent runs follows one run through them.
flowchart TB B["Browser"] -->|HTTPS| CP subgraph inst["Instance namespace"] direction LR CP["Control plane"] -->|PolicyWatch| GW["Gateway"] end subgraph sbx["Sandbox namespace"] SB["Sandbox pod
runtime + harness"] --- PVC[("Task volume")] end SB -->|agent channel| CP SB -->|proxy, Git| GW CP --> DB[("PostgreSQL")] CP -->|API| FORGE["Forge"] GW -->|Git| FORGE GW --> EXT["Allowed hosts"]
data.components#Components: Component Runs as Does Holds Control plane Deployment dark-factory serve Web UI, task and run scheduling, the agent channel for sandboxes, forge plugins, sandbox provisioning, policy distribution to the gateway The database connection; resolves credentials from Secret references when it uses them Gateway Deployment dark-factory gateway (2 or more replicas) Egress proxy for sandbox HTTP(S), Git smart-HTTP proxy with push checks, inference endpoint for model traffic, live traffic events No database access and no Kubernetes token; policies and forge and model provider credentials arrive from the control plane and stay in memory migrate job Helm pre-install and pre-upgrade hook Schema migrations, application role and grants The owner role’s password Sandbox pod Pod per run in the sandbox namespace, Kata Containers where configured The project image with the runtime (factory-agent) and the harness (for example Claude Code over ACP) mounted as image volumes The task volume at /data; no credential PostgreSQL External All state: projects, personas, tasks, runs, transcripts and their binary content, requests, egress rules, audit log The control plane and the gateway are the same binary in two modes. The control plane can run with several replicas: every replica serves the UI and agent connections and can start runs (the database prevents two runs of one task); jobs that must run once, such as the task volume cleanup, run on the replica holding the instance lease.
data.connections#Connections: From To Protocol Authentication Browser Control plane :8080 HTTPS through your ingress or Gateway API route OIDC login, server-side session Sandbox Control plane :9443 (agent port) gRPC, bidirectional stream mTLS: a per-pod certificate from cert-manager’s CSI driver, checked against the pod’s IP and UID Sandbox Gateway :3128 (proxy) HTTP CONNECT and plain HTTP proxying Source pod IP, looked up in the sandbox registry Sandbox Gateway :8443 (Git) Git smart HTTP over HTTPS (instance CA) Source pod IP; the path names the task Gateway Control plane :9444 (internal) gRPC (PolicyWatch, push records, events) mTLS Control plane Gateway :9444 (internal) gRPC Tail for the live traffic view mTLS Control plane Forge API HTTPS from a forge plugin The project’s forge credential, added by the control plane Gateway Forge Git HTTPS The project’s forge credential, injected by the Git proxy Sandboxes resolve no DNS names: the proxy and control plane addresses are passed as IPs, and the generated NetworkPolicy of each run allows only the control plane, the gateway and explicitly allowed cluster services. Details: Security.
data.design-records#Design records: The decisions behind this layout are recorded as ADRs in the repository, for example ADR-0029 (egress gateway), ADR-0030 (Kubernetes only) and ADR-0013 (single-tenant instances).
data.kubernetes-footprint#Kubernetes footprin: Namespace Contains Created by Instance (for example dark-factory) Control plane, gateway, migrate job, Services, Secrets with credentials, Leases the Helm release Sandbox (for example dark-factory-sandboxes) Sandbox pods, task volumes (PVCs), generated per-run NetworkPolicies the chart (sandboxNamespace.create) or you; never the control plane The control plane gets the permissions it needs in these two namespaces only: pods, PVCs, NetworkPolicies and events (read) in the sandbox namespace; leases, Secrets (read) and EndpointSlices in the instance namespace. The gateway and sandbox pods get no Kubernetes API token. At startup the control plane checks its permissions and refuses to start if one is missing.

data: A task is a unit of work for one persona in one project. A run is one sandbox lifetime that works on a task: it starts when the task has something to do (a new task, a message, a resume time that passed) and ends when the agent is done, waits too long for an answer, or is stopped. A task usually has several runs. Its code lives in Git, on the branch factory/task/; the task volume only caches the checkout between runs.
data.agent-tools#Agent tools:
The control plane gives every run the factory tools of contract/mcp/factory-tools.v2.json; the harness sees them as the MCP server factory. Calls are executed by the control plane, scoped to the run’s task, and at most once per call_id.
Tool Purpose update_pull_request, comment_on_issue, report_progress, set_task_title Shape the pull request, comment on the linked issue, set the status line and the title complete_task Ends the run after the turn; the task goes to review ask_question, request_approval Requests to the humans of the task read_pull_request_feedback, comment_on_pull_request Read and answer reviews create_task, list_personas, send_message Delegation: create tasks for other personas, list them, message a child. create_task creates tasks only in the run’s project; send_message acts only on children of the run’s task write_artifact, list_artifacts, read_artifact Artifacts: write named text and image files on the own task, list and read those of related tasks
data.continuation-across-runs#Continuation ac: Every run after the first gets the harness session id of the previous run and a summary of the task’s transcript: title, description, user messages, agent messages and one line per tool call, capped in size. A harness that can resume its session (Claude Code) continues it; others start from the summary. The workspace comes from the task branch, the WIP snapshot and the cached checkout on the task volume.
data.how-a-run-ends#How a run ends: Outcome Task status afterwards completed (the agent called complete_task) in_review; the pull request is marked ready and gets the completion summary of this run (see Pull request actions) end_turn (idle deadline passed) waiting blocked (a blocking question was not answered in time) blocked rate_limited (the model provider’s usage limit) rate_limited, with a resume time; the next run starts automatically and continues limit_reached (a budget, or the harness’s token or turn limit) limit_reached sandbox_lost, connect_timeout, provisioning_failed queued again with a growing delay, up to runs.maxAutoResumes (default 3) times; then failed cancelled (stopped by a human, or over the wall-clock budget) waiting; a cancelled task stays cancelled, a task marked done stays completed failed failed If messages are still undelivered at the end of a run, the task becomes queued instead, so the next run picks them up.
data.one-run#One run: sequenceDiagram autonumber participant UI as Web UI / DB participant CP as Control plane participant K as Kubernetes participant R as Runtime (sandbox) participant H as Harness participant G as Gateway participant DB as Database participant O as Outbox dispatcher participant F as Forge UI->>CP: task queued (new task or message) CP->>K: task volume task-, sandbox pod, NetworkPolicy K-->>CP: pod started (pod IP) R->>CP: connect (mTLS), Hello CP->>R: Assign (gateway URL, placeholder key), Prompts R->>G: clone or fetch through the Git proxy G->>F: forward with the forge credential H->>G: model requests (placeholder key) G->>CP: usage records R->>H: start session (new or resumed) loop each turn R->>H: prompt (messages with author lines) H-->>R: updates (messages, tool calls) R->>CP: transcript events R->>G: push factory/task/ (push checks) R->>CP: push report opt first commit ahead of base CP->>DB: enqueue pr.sync (same transaction as the push report) end opt held-back messages after persisted TurnEnded CP->>R: Prompts (all released messages) end end Note over CP,R: waits for messages until the idle deadline CP->>R: Release (or Cancel) R->>G: push task branch, WIP snapshot R->>CP: run report (outcome, workspace state) CP->>K: delete pod (volume stays) CP->>DB: enqueue pr.sync (open if pushed, ready if completed) with the run end O->>F: open draft pull request, mark it ready, post the completion summary (retried) Scheduling. A task is due when it is queued (or rate_limited) and its resume time has passed. Up to runs.maxConcurrent runs (default 4) are active at a time; further due tasks wait, oldest first. A task never has two active runs. Provisioning. The control plane ensures the task volume exists, creates the sandbox pod (the project’s image with the runtime and harness mounted read-only, the configured runtime class) and a NetworkPolicy for the run. Connecting. The runtime dials the control plane with its pod certificate. The control plane resolves the certificate to the run and sends the Assign: repository URL through the Git proxy, branches, commit identity, system prompt, harness settings, the harness environment (the gateway’s inference endpoint as base URL, a placeholder API key and the instance CA; no credential), budgets and the continuation of earlier runs (harness session id and a transcript summary). Preparing. The runtime clones or updates the workspace through the Git proxy and writes its own .git/config; anything left on the volume is treated as untrusted. Turns. The harness works on the prompt. Every message and tool call is streamed to the control plane and stored as the task’s transcript. After a turn with new commits the runtime pushes the task branch. The first push ahead of the base branch enqueues the draft pull request; an outbox job opens it (see Pull request actions). All messages waiting at turn start form one harness input, in queue order. Each starts with the same readable author name as in the UI and a colon, for example Peter Kurfer: or Task assignment:. A continuation summary stays first. Waiting. Between turns the run waits for messages. A message queued in the UI reaches the agent at the next turn boundary without a new run. Messages released together arrive in one Prompts control message, including after reconnects, so they start one turn. After runs.keepAliveSeconds (default 600) without a message, the control plane releases the run. Finalizing. The runtime stops the harness, pushes the task branch, writes a WIP snapshot of uncommitted files to factory/wip/ and reports the outcome. The control plane deletes the pod; the task volume stays for the next run.
data.pull-request-actions#Pull request action:
The control plane never calls the forge from the agent stream. Opening the draft pull request, marking it ready and posting the completion summary are pr.sync jobs of the outbox, enqueued in the transaction that records their trigger and run by the dispatcher on the leader replica:
Trigger Job Push of the task branch ahead of the base branch, task without a pull request open the draft pull request End of a run that pushed the task branch open the draft pull request if it is still missing End of a run with outcome completed mark the pull request ready and post the summary of that run Mark done in the UI, task with a pull request mark the pull request ready, no summary Failed forge calls are retried with backoff (30 s doubling to 10 min) for one hour, also after a control plane restart; then the job is given up with a warning (df.outbox.jobs{kind="pr.sync",result="gave_up"}). Behavior to know:
A completed run that never pushed the task branch opens no pull request. A pull request an earlier run opened is still marked ready. The summary comes from the run’s own complete_task call (runs.completion_summary); a run without one posts none. A retry after a failed comment call may post it twice. Ready and summary go to the pull request recorded on the task. A message queued after the completion or after Mark done keeps the pull request a draft. The summary is still posted. Both times come from the database clock under the task lock, so they are ordered like the lock. A cancelled task gets no pull request action.
data.task-volumes#Task volumes: Each task has one volume (task-), mounted at /data. It is a cache: committed work is in Git, uncommitted work in the WIP snapshot. Volumes of tasks closed for 7 days, or idle for 30 days, are deleted hourly (volumes.retainAfterCloseSeconds, volumes.idleTtlSeconds), the volume of a task whose pull request was merged at the next hourly check; Reset workspace in a task’s status menu deletes one on demand. The next run re-clones.

data:
The web UI logs users in through an OIDC provider. The control plane is a confidential OIDC client (authorization code flow with PKCE, performed server-side). Browsers only get an HTTP-only session cookie; tokens stay on the server. Every UI page requires the role board-member, read from a flat claim of the ID token. The lifecycle event subscriptions of a project (tab “Lifecycle events” of the project’s edit dialog) also require the role admin.
sequenceDiagram participant B as Browser participant C as Control plane participant P as OIDC provider B->>C: GET /tasks (no session) C-->>B: 303 /login?next=/tasks B->>C: GET /login C-->>B: 303 provider /auth (state, nonce, PKCE challenge) B->>P: log in P-->>B: 302 /auth/callback?code&state B->>C: GET /auth/callback C->>P: POST /token (code, PKCE verifier, client secret) P-->>C: ID token (role claim), refresh token C-->>B: 303 /tasks + session cookie Provider guides:
Keycloak: client role board-member in a roles claim. Dex: group board-member in the groups claim. Authentik: group board-member in the groups claim.
data.control-plane-settings#Control plane set:
The chart renders the auth section of config.yaml from the oidc.* values (chart README):
Field Helm value Required Default Effect auth.issuerUrl oidc.issuerUrl yes Issuer; /.well-known/openid-configuration is discovered below it on every login, callback and refresh. auth.clientId oidc.clientId yes dark-factory (chart) OIDC client ID. auth.clientSecretFile oidc.existingSecret, oidc.clientSecretKey yes File with the client secret (the chart mounts the Secret at /run/secrets/oidc/client-secret). auth.publicUrl oidc.publicUrl yes Externally visible base URL; the redirect URI is /auth/callback, the post-logout redirect /. Must be https://; plain http:// is accepted only on loopback (localhost, 127.0.0.0/8, ::1) for local development, and then the session cookie is sent without Secure. serve refuses any other http:// URL. auth.rolesClaim oidc.rolesClaim no roles Top-level ID token claim with the role list. auth.extraScopes oidc.extraScopes no [] Scopes requested in addition to openid and profile, for example [groups, offline_access] for Dex. Without an auth section (oidc.publicUrl empty) dark-factory serve logs a warning, serves only /healthz, /readyz and /assets/*, and the UI is unavailable.
Roles are read at every login and every token refresh; they are never stored as the source of truth. A role removed at the provider takes effect when the access token expires and is refreshed. Live views (task list, task detail) reconnect at that point, so they stop as well.
data.verify#Verify: Open https:///. You are redirected to the provider and, after login, to /tasks. A user without board-member sees 403 with the message Your account lacks the role board-member. A user with board-member but without admin sees no tab “Lifecycle events” in the project’s edit dialog, and requests for the project’s subscriptions (/projects//subscriptions) answer 403 with Your account lacks the role admin. Log out deletes the server-side session and ends the provider session (RP-initiated logout).

data: Authentik as the OIDC provider. Dark Factory reads Authentik group names from the top-level groups claim of the ID token. Members of board-member may use the UI; members of admin may also manage lifecycle event subscriptions. How login works and every control plane setting: Authentication.
In the Authentik admin interface, select Applications > Applications > Create. Create an OAuth2/OpenID Connect provider and application with these settings:
Setting Value Application name Dark Factory Slug dark-factory Client type Confidential Client ID dark-factory (auth.clientId) Redirect URI Strict, Authorization: https://factory.example.org/auth/callback Redirect URI Strict, Post Logout: https://factory.example.org/ Signing key Select an available signing key Keep the authorization-code flow enabled. Copy the provider’s client secret into a Kubernetes Secret in the instance namespace:
kubectl -n dark-factory create secret generic dark-factory-oidc \ --from-literal=client-secret='' Authentik versions before 2026.5 treat every redirect URI as an authorization URI. On those versions, configure only https://factory.example.org/auth/callback; do not add the post-logout URI.
data.2-provide-the-groups-claim#2. Provide th:
Create the Authentik groups board-member and, if users manage lifecycle event subscriptions, admin. Add the appropriate users to them. A user with only admin cannot open the Dark Factory UI; they also need board-member.
Under the provider’s selected scopes, add a scope mapping named groups that returns the user’s group names. Its claim must be a top-level list in the ID token, for example:
{ "groups": ["board-member", "admin"] } The group names must match exactly. Dark Factory compares the claim values as strings. If you use an Authentik property mapping instead of the default group mapping, make it return the group names, not display labels or nested objects.
data.3-configure-the-control-plane#3. Configu:
The issuer URL is the provider URL with the application slug. It must include its trailing slash. Helm values (all settings: Control plane settings):
oidc: issuerUrl: https://auth.example.org/application/o/dark-factory/ clientId: dark-factory existingSecret: dark-factory-oidc clientSecretKey: client-secret publicUrl: https://factory.example.org rolesClaim: groups extraScopes: [groups] This example requests the groups scope but not offline_access. Authentik issues a refresh token only when the provider includes an offline_access scope mapping and the client requests that scope. Without a refresh token, the Dark Factory session ends when the ID token expires.
Then check the login as in Verify.
data.troubleshooting#Troubleshooting: Symptom Cause Authentik rejects the redirect URI The authorization callback does not exactly match oidc.publicUrl + /auth/callback, or a pre-2026.5 provider also has a post-logout URI. 403 for a user in the group The groups claim is absent from the ID token, oidc.rolesClaim differs from the claim name, or the user is not in a group named exactly board-member. Login unavailable (502) The control plane cannot reach oidc.issuerUrl; check the NetworkPolicy and issuer URL. Logged out when the ID token expires offline_access is not requested or its scope mapping is missing, so Authentik did not issue a refresh token.

data: Dex as the OIDC provider. Dex has no roles: the control plane reads the groups claim instead, so the users who may operate the factory are members of the group board-member. Dex passes the groups on from its connector (for example LDAP or an upstream OIDC provider). How the login works and every control plane setting: Authentication.
data.1-register-the-client#1. Register the cl:
Add a static client to the Dex configuration:
staticClients: - id: dark-factory name: Dark Factory secret: redirectURIs: - https://factory.example.org/auth/callback postLogoutRedirectURIs: - https://factory.example.org/ Store the same secret in the instance namespace:
kubectl -n dark-factory create secret generic dark-factory-oidc \ --from-literal=client-secret=''
data.2-provide-the-group#2. Provide the group:
The ID token must contain "groups": ["board-member", …]. Where the group comes from depends on the connector:
Connector Group board-member LDAP an LDAP group named board-member (groupSearch of the connector) OIDC (upstream) the upstream groups claim (insecureEnableGroups: true on the connector) Static passwords groups of the user entry; for tests only The group name must be exactly board-member: the control plane compares the claim values as strings. The GitHub connector names every team group : (for example acme:board-member), so it cannot provide the group; use Keycloak or another connector instead.
Users who manage the lifecycle event subscriptions of projects also need a group named exactly admin, provided the same way. They find the subscriptions in the tab “Lifecycle events” of a project’s edit dialog.
data.3-configure-the-control-plane#3. Configu:
Dex returns groups only for the scope groups, and a refresh token only for offline_access. Without a refresh token the session ends when the ID token expires.
oidc: issuerUrl: https://dex.example.org/dex clientId: dark-factory existingSecret: dark-factory-oidc clientSecretKey: client-secret publicUrl: https://factory.example.org rolesClaim: groups extraScopes: [groups, offline_access] issuerUrl must match the issuer of the Dex configuration exactly, including the path. Then check the login as in Verify.
The local development setup (just serve-local, dev/dex.yaml) uses the same settings with static users (development guide).
data.troubleshooting#Troubleshooting: Symptom Cause Unregistered redirect_uri at Dex The redirect URI does not match oidc.publicUrl + /auth/callback. 403 for a user in the group groups is missing in the scopes (oidc.extraScopes), the connector does not pass groups, or the group name is not exactly board-member. Login unavailable (502) The control plane cannot reach oidc.issuerUrl, or it differs from the Dex issuer. Logged out when the ID token expires offline_access is missing in oidc.extraScopes.

data: Keycloak as the OIDC provider: a confidential client dark-factory and its client roles board-member and admin in a top-level roles claim of the ID token. How the login works and every control plane setting: Authentication.
data.1-create-the-client#1. Create the client:
In the realm of your instance, Clients > Create client:
Setting Value Client type OpenID Connect Client ID dark-factory (auth.clientId) Client authentication On (confidential client) Authentication flow Standard flow only; turn off direct access grants and implicit flow Valid redirect URIs https:///auth/callback Valid post logout redirect URIs https:/// Web origins empty Under Advanced > Advanced settings set Proof Key for Code Exchange Code Challenge Method to S256.
Copy the client secret from the client’s Credentials tab into a Kubernetes Secret in the instance namespace:
kubectl -n dark-factory create secret generic dark-factory-oidc \ --from-literal=client-secret=''
data.2-create-the-roles-and-map-them-into-the:
Clients > dark-factory > Roles > Create role: name board-member. Assign it to the users (or a group) who may operate the factory.
Create role again: name admin. Assign it to the users who manage the lifecycle event subscriptions of projects. They find them in the tab “Lifecycle events” of a project’s edit dialog, which other users do not see. They need board-member as well; admin alone opens no page.
Clients > dark-factory > Client scopes > dark-factory-dedicated > Configure a new mapper > User Client Role (one mapper; it puts every client role of the user into the claim):
Setting Value Name roles Client ID dark-factory Multivalued On Token Claim Name roles (auth.rolesClaim) Claim JSON Type String Add to ID token On Add to access token optional The default resource_access.dark-factory.roles claim is nested and is not read. The claim must be a top-level list, for example "roles": ["board-member", "admin"].
A role removed in Keycloak takes effect when the access token expires (default 5 minutes) and is refreshed.
Revoke Refresh Token (refresh token rotation) is supported: the control plane refreshes each session once, even when several requests arrive with an expired token at the same time.
data.3-configure-the-control-plane#3. Configu:
Helm values (all settings: Control plane settings):
oidc: issuerUrl: https://id.example.org/realms/dark-factory clientId: dark-factory existingSecret: dark-factory-oidc clientSecretKey: client-secret publicUrl: https://factory.example.org rolesClaim: roles Then check the login as in Verify.
data.troubleshooting#Troubleshooting: Symptom Cause Invalid parameter: redirect_uri at Keycloak The redirect URI does not match auth.publicUrl + /auth/callback. 403 for a user who has the role The mapper does not add the claim to the ID token, or auth.rolesClaim differs from Token Claim Name. Login unavailable (502) The control plane cannot reach auth.issuerUrl; check the NetworkPolicy and the issuer URL. Login failed (400) The login state does not match, e.g. the login page was opened in another browser or the cookie was blocked. Logged out every few minutes The refresh was refused: the Keycloak SSO session or refresh token expired, or the client lost Standard flow.

data:
An instance keeps all its state in one PostgreSQL database (version 17, the version the tests run against). Dark Factory separates the privileges between two roles:
Role Helm value (default) Used by Rights Owner database.owner.user (dark_factory_owner) only the migrate job (pre-install and pre-upgrade hook) owns the database and the schema database.schema (dark_factory), runs the migrations, grants the application role its rights Application database.app.user (dark_factory_app) dark-factory serve SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE on the tables, USAGE, SELECT on sequences, append-only (SELECT, INSERT) on audit_log; no DDL Each password lives in a Secret in the instance namespace:
Secret (Helm value, default) Key Mounted into database.owner.existingSecret (dark-factory-db-owner) password (database.owner.passwordKey) the migrate job database.app.existingSecret (dark-factory-db-app) password (database.app.passwordKey) the control plane; also the migrate job when it manages the application role kubectl -n dark-factory create secret generic dark-factory-db-owner --from-literal=password='' kubectl -n dark-factory create secret generic dark-factory-db-app --from-literal=password=''
data.connection-settings#Connection settings: database: host: postgres.databases.svc port: 5432 database: dark_factory schema: dark_factory maxConnections: 16 # pool size of the control plane All database values: chart README.
data.option-a-the-migration-job-manages-the-a:
Only the owner exists beforehand, and it needs CREATEROLE:
CREATE ROLE dark_factory_owner LOGIN PASSWORD '' CREATEROLE; CREATE DATABASE dark_factory OWNER dark_factory_owner; On every install and upgrade the migrate job creates the application role (or sets its password from the Secret, which rotates it) and applies the grants. Helm values: none, database.migrate.manageAppRole is true by default.
data.option-b-both-roles-provisioned-outside-:
For declarative setups (CloudNativePG managed roles, Crossplane, Terraform, a DBA) where the owner must not have CREATEROLE. Create both roles as plain LOGIN roles:
CREATE ROLE dark_factory_owner LOGIN PASSWORD ''; CREATE ROLE dark_factory_app LOGIN PASSWORD ''; CREATE DATABASE dark_factory OWNER dark_factory_owner; \connect dark_factory CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS dark_factory AUTHORIZATION dark_factory_owner; Instead of owning the database, the owner may hold CREATE and CONNECT (with GRANT OPTION on CONNECT) on it. Then disable role management:
database: migrate: manageAppRole: false The migrate job still re-applies all grants to the existing application role on every install and upgrade; it only stops creating the role and setting its password.

data:
This guide installs one Dark Factory instance into a Kubernetes cluster with the Helm chart of a release. It ends with a working login. Dark Factory is pre-MVP: pin the chart version and read the release notes before you upgrade.
flowchart LR A[Prerequisites] --> B[PostgreSQL roles] B --> C[OIDC client] C --> D[Secrets] D --> E[helm install] E --> F[First login]
data.1-create-the-postgresql-roles#1. Create:
Dark Factory uses two roles: an owner that runs the migrations and an application role that serves requests (no DDL rights). The simplest setup lets the migration job manage the application role. Then only the owner needs to exist, and it needs CREATEROLE:
CREATE ROLE dark_factory_owner LOGIN PASSWORD '' CREATEROLE; CREATE DATABASE dark_factory OWNER dark_factory_owner; Put both passwords into Secrets in the instance namespace (the application password is set on the role by the migration job):
kubectl create namespace dark-factory kubectl -n dark-factory create secret generic dark-factory-db-owner --from-literal=password='' kubectl -n dark-factory create secret generic dark-factory-db-app --from-literal=password='' If you provision roles declaratively and the owner must not have CREATEROLE, create both roles yourself: see Database.
data.2-create-the-oidc-client#2. Create the O:
Create the confidential client dark-factory and provide board-member in a top-level role or group claim of the ID token. The steps are in Keycloak, Authentik, and Dex. At the end you have a client secret; store it:
kubectl -n dark-factory create secret generic dark-factory-oidc --from-literal=client-secret=''
data.3-write-the-helm-values#3. Write the Hel:
values.yaml for a cluster with Kata Containers, an external PostgreSQL and Keycloak:
database: host: postgres.databases.svc database: dark_factory oidc: issuerUrl: https://id.example.org/realms/dark-factory publicUrl: https://factory.example.org sandboxNamespace: runtimeClassName: kata # Publish the UI through an existing Gateway API Gateway. httpRoute: enabled: true parentRefs: - name: public namespace: gateway-system hostnames: - factory.example.org networkPolicy: ingressController: namespaceSelector: kubernetes.io/metadata.name: gateway-system Everything else has a default; the chart README lists every key. Set oidc.publicUrl to the URL the browser uses: without it the web UI stays unavailable.
data.4-install#4. Install:
Pin the version. Releases are named YYYY.M.N (for example 2026.11.0); the list is on the GitHub releases page.
helm install dark-factory oci://ghcr.io/prskr/dark-factory/charts/dark-factory \ --namespace dark-factory \ --version 2026.11.0 \ --values values.yaml The chart runs the migrate job first (pre-install hook), then starts the control plane and the gateway. Check that both are ready:
kubectl -n dark-factory get pods kubectl -n dark-factory rollout status deploy/dark-factory-control-plane The images default to the chart’s appVersion, so the images match the chart version.
data.5-first-login#5. First login: Give your user the board-member role or group described by your provider’s guide. Open the oidc.publicUrl. You are redirected to the provider and, after the login, to the task list. The profile menu (your initials) shows the version of the running instance and links to the docs of exactly that version. A user without the role gets 403; other symptoms are in the provider’s troubleshooting table.
data.next-steps#Next steps: Using Dark Factory: credentials, projects and personas, then the first task. Forges: connect your Forgejo or GitHub repositories. Security: what the sandbox can and cannot do. Observability: log format and levels, metrics and traces.
data.prerequisites#Prerequisites: What Why Kubernetes 1.36 or newer The runtime and the harness reach sandboxes as image volumes (kubeVersion of the chart). Kata Containers with a RuntimeClass (this guide: kata) Sandboxes run untrusted agent code and should run in a microVM. Without it they run in the cluster’s default runtime. cert-manager (with the CSI driver) Issues the mTLS certificates of the control plane, the gateway and every sandbox. A CNI that enforces NetworkPolicy (Cilium or any other) Sandboxes may only reach the gateway; the chart ships a default-deny policy. PostgreSQL 17, reachable from the cluster The only state of an instance (the version the tests run against). An OIDC provider: Keycloak (this guide), Authentik, or Dex Login to the web UI. A Gateway API Gateway (or any other way to publish port 8080 of the control plane) with a TLS certificate The browser needs an HTTPS URL; it is also the OIDC redirect target. helm 3.8 or newer and access to ghcr.io/prskr/dark-factory The chart is an OCI artifact.
data.upgrade#Upgrade: Run helm upgrade with the new --version and the same values. The migration job runs again before the new control plane starts. Read the release notes first.

data:
Dark Factory talks to external systems through plugins: WebAssembly components that run inside the control plane in a sandbox (Wasmtime). A plugin sees no credentials; the control plane adds them to each request and limits the plugin to the hosts of its route.
Forges: Forgejo and GitHub, for pull requests, issues and review feedback; forge webhooks wake tasks on reviews, mentions, merges and CI failures. Outgoing, without a plugin:
Lifecycle events: signed webhooks when a task volume or a run sandbox is created or destroyed.

A forge plugin opens and updates the draft pull request of a task, comments on issues and reads review feedback. Agents never call the forge API: the control plane calls it with the project’s forge credential. Git clone and push go through the gateway’s Git proxy.
Forge Plugin Default route Forgejo forgejo every host no other plugin claims (default plugin) GitHub, GitHub Enterprise Server github github.com How a project’s repository host selects a plugin, the instance configuration keys and the GitHub how-tos: Plugin configuration. Waking tasks on reviews, mentions, merges and CI failures: Forge webhooks.
data.connect-a-repository#Connect a repositor:
Create a token for a bot account with write access to the repository. What works depends on the account’s access level, see Bot account access:
Forgejo: scopes write:repository, write:issue and read:user. With write access only, the review loop works but every human reviewer counts as outside; make the account repository admin for correct roles (token scopes). GitHub: a fine-grained token with Pull requests, Issues and Contents read/write and Metadata read (connect a GitHub repository). Store it in a Secret in the instance namespace:
kubectl -n dark-factory create secret generic forge-token --from-file=token= In the web UI, Settings → Credentials → New credential reference: a name, Secret forge-token, key token. The control plane stores only the reference, never the token.
Projects → New project: the repository URL (https://git.example.org//.git) and that credential as forge credential. The hint below the URL names the plugin that serves it.
data.plugin-images#Plugin images:
Each plugin ships as its own image (FROM scratch, one file /plugin.wasm). The kubelet pulls it and the control plane pod mounts it read-only as an image volume at /plugins/. The images follow the chart version (appVersion) unless pinned:
plugins: forgejo: image: digest: sha256:0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef Upgrade a plugin: set the new plugins..image.tag (or digest) and run helm upgrade. The control plane rolls; a plugin image that cannot be pulled keeps the new pod in ContainerCreating while the old pods keep serving.
Cluster without image volumes: build a control plane image that contains the component and set a path instead of an image:
FROM ghcr.io/prskr/dark-factory/control-plane:2026.11.0 COPY plugin.wasm /custom/forgejo.wasm image: controlPlane: repository: registry.example.org/control-plane-with-plugin plugins: forgejo: image: null path: /custom/forgejo.wasm Instance without GitHub: plugins.github: null removes the entry; projects on github.com then go to the default plugin.
All plugin values: chart README.
data.review-feedback#Review feedback:
The agent reads the reviews on its pull request with the tool read_pull_request_feedback: PR comments, reviews (verdict, body) and review threads (thread id, path, line, resolved flag, review comments). Every item carries its author’s login and role:
Role Meaning bot the factory’s own account member write access to the repository or more outside anyone else, and authors whose role the forge would not tell the bot account (Bot account access) The agent treats the content of outside items as untrusted and asks a member to confirm before it follows their instructions.
Each list is ordered by last activity, newest first. A comment or review edited after a newer item was written comes first. The result carries next_since; the agent passes it as since on its next read to get only what changed. next_since is the newest activity in the result minus 5 minutes, never earlier than the since that was passed, and always written in UTC (...Z). The overlap covers items written while the plugin was still listing, so items of the last minutes come back unchanged. An edited comment or review keeps its id but has a new updated_at, and a thread with a new reply keeps its thread id. The agent therefore skips a comment or review whose id and updated_at it already handled, and for a returned thread reads only the review comments it has not seen.
Scenario: the agent reads the feedback at 10:20 for the first time. The newest item, a review comment, is from 10:15:00Z, so next_since is 2026-11-05T10:10:00Z. After a review wakes the task, the agent reads with since = 2026-11-05T10:10:00Z and gets the review comment again (skipped by its id and updated_at) plus everything newer.
The result stays within a size budget of 48 KiB. When it does not fit, whole items are left out, oldest last activity first, and truncated is true. Items left out are not returned by later reads with next_since; the agent opens the pull request URL if it needs older context. Forgejo needs one request per review for its review comments, so a call reads them for the 20 newest reviews only, and sets truncated when there are more. The wake message of a webhook tells the agent to pass its last next_since as since (Forge webhooks).
data.troubleshooting#Troubleshooting: Symptom Cause The control plane pod does not start; kubectl describe pod shows a failed pull of the volume plugin- The plugin image or tag does not exist, the registry needs credentials (image.pullSecrets apply to plugin images too), or the cluster has no image volume support. A project fails with a config error naming a plugin That plugin did not load (log event “forge plugin not loaded” with the reason). Its projects never fall back to another plugin. serve stops at startup A host claimed by two plugins, two plugins without hosts, an apiUrl without https://, or no forge plugin loaded at all (Startup). A tool call fails with “the forge refused the request (GET /api/v1/…: …)” The forge answered 401 or 403. The message names the request and the forge’s reason: a token without the scope, or an account without access to the repository (Refused requests). Every human reviewer is outside and the log has “cannot read the repository permission of …” The bot account may not read repository permissions (Forgejo: needs repository admin). The review loop works; the wake policy members never wakes (Bot account access).

data:
Section plugins of the instance configuration (/etc/dark-factory/config.yaml) is a map from plugin name to its settings. The host does not know plugin-specific keys; settings is passed through to the plugin as wasi:config/store. hosts and authScheme are host-side keys: the host enforces them, the plugin never sees them.
plugins: forgejo: path: /plugins/forgejo/plugin.wasm callTimeoutSeconds: 30 memoryMib: 64 settings: wip-prefixes: "WIP:,[WIP]" # no hosts: default plugin github: path: /plugins/github/plugin.wasm authScheme: bearer hosts: - host: github.com apiUrl: https://api.github.com - host: ghe.example.org apiUrl: https://ghe.example.org/api/v3 Key Required Default Effect plugins..path yes none Component file. plugins..callTimeoutSeconds no 30 Upper bound of one plugin call (retries excluded); at least 1 and at most 300, any other value fails startup naming the key. read_pull_request_feedback assumes a call is shorter than its 5-minute next_since overlap, see Review feedback. Guest code is stopped by epoch interruption (50 ms granularity), network waits by a timeout. A timed-out call fails with internal; the instance is discarded. plugins..memoryMib no 64 Linear memory limit per instance. Exceeding it fails the call with internal. plugins..hosts no [] Repository hosts this plugin serves. Each entry is a string host[:port] or a map {host, apiUrl}; the map rejects unknown keys. Hosts are DNS names, IPv4 or bracketed IPv6 addresses; they are lowercased, a trailing dot and port 443 are dropped, any other port stays part of the host. A host may be claimed by one entry only. An entry without hosts (or with []) is the default plugin; at most one is allowed. plugins..hosts[].apiUrl no https:// API base URL for this host. Must start with https:// and have no userinfo, query or fragment; host lowercased, port 443 and a trailing / dropped, the path is kept (https://ghe.example.org/api/v3). Becomes the plugin’s base-url and the only authority its requests may reach. Only valid in the {host, apiUrl} form, which rejects unknown keys. plugins..authScheme no token How the project’s forge credential is sent: token → Authorization: token , bearer → Authorization: Bearer . The host sets the header on every request and replaces one set by the plugin. Applies to all hosts of the entry, the default plugin included. plugins..settings no {} String map handed to the plugin unchanged. The host adds base-url (the route’s apiUrl; for the default plugin scheme and authority of the project’s repo_url) and it wins over a configured one. Keys are documented by the plugin (Forgejo: wip-prefixes, see plugins/forgejo/README.md; GitHub: draft-mode, wip-prefixes, api-version, see plugins/github/README.md). plugins..webhookSecretFile no unset File with the shared secret the forge signs webhooks with (HMAC-SHA256), read once at startup; trailing line breaks are dropped. Set, it enables POST /webhooks/; unset, that endpoint answers 404. The secret stays in the host: plugins check signatures through webhook-signature.verify. The Helm chart sets it from plugins..webhookSecret. Unknown keys fail parsing the configuration. An unknown authScheme value fails startup naming the plugin and the value (see “Startup”).
The Helm chart renders the section from its plugins.* values and mounts each plugin image (//deploy:plugin_forgejo_image, one file /plugin.wasm) as an image volume at /plugins/ (deploy/helm/dark-factory/README.md, “Plugins”). All plugins share one Wasmtime engine and epoch clock.
data.add-a-second-forge#Add a second forge:
Make the component available to the control plane (for the chart: a plugin image mounted at /plugins/).
Add an entry with the hosts it serves, the apiUrl where the API is not at https://, and the authScheme the forge expects. Give the existing entry hosts as well, so neither is a catch-all:
plugins: forgejo: path: /plugins/forgejo/plugin.wasm hosts: [git.example.org] github: path: /plugins/github/plugin.wasm authScheme: bearer hosts: - host: github.com apiUrl: https://api.github.com Restart serve and check the “forge route” events: each host with the expected plugin and available=true.
Create projects with a repo_url on the new host and a forge credential for that forge.
data.add-github-enterprise-server#Add GitHub:
Add the host with its API URL. Settings apply to every host of an entry. A server older than the default API version 2026-03-10 needs api-version: "2022-11-28"; in the github entry that setting would also apply to github.com, so give the server its own entry with the same component:
plugins: github: path: /plugins/github/plugin.wasm authScheme: bearer hosts: - host: github.com apiUrl: https://api.github.com github-enterprise: path: /plugins/github/plugin.wasm authScheme: bearer hosts: - host: ghe.example.org apiUrl: https://ghe.example.org/api/v3 settings: api-version: "2022-11-28" Otherwise add {host: ghe.example.org, apiUrl: https://ghe.example.org/api/v3} to the github entry’s hosts. GraphQL goes to https://ghe.example.org/api/graphql without further configuration.
Restart serve and check the “forge route” event for ghe.example.org.
Connect repositories as above, with a token from the server, repository URLs https://ghe.example.org//.git and an egress rule for ghe.example.org. With a separate entry, the web UI shows these projects with the generic Git icon and the hint names that entry (“Served by the github-enterprise integration; …”).
data.bot-account-access#Bot account access:
The forge credential of a project belongs to a bot account. What the factory can do depends on the account’s access to the repository, not only on the token scopes. Three levels matter:
Forgejo
Access of the account PR create and update Comments list-feedback Author roles Webhook policy members Read no (unauthorized) no (unauthorized) works; every human is outside every human is outside never wakes Write yes yes works; every human is outside every human is outside never wakes Repository admin yes yes works member for write, admin and owner permission, else outside works GitHub
Access of the account PR create and update Comments list-feedback Author roles Webhook policy members Read no (unauthorized) no (unauthorized) works; owners, members and collaborators are outside those are outside never wakes Write (or admin) yes yes works member for write and admin permission, else outside works The role of an author comes from the repository permission lookup (GET .../collaborators/{login}/permission). Forgejo answers it with 403 unless the account is a site or repository admin; GitHub needs push access. When the forge refuses the lookup (403), the plugin does not fail the call. The author is outside, the agent treats the content as untrusted, and a project with the wake policy members does not wake the task for that author. The plugin writes one warning per author and call to stderr, logged at warn as event “plugin stderr” with the field plugin and the text below in line:
Forge Warning Forgejo warning: cannot read the repository permission of : the bot account needs repository admin; treating as outside GitHub warning: cannot read the repository permission of : treating as outside So with a Forgejo bot account that has write access only, the review loop works, but every human reviewer is outside. Make the bot account repository admin to get correct roles.
GET .../collaborators/{login} (answers 204 or 404) is not used as a fallback: it needs only read access, but Forgejo answers 404 for the repository owner and for members of the owning organisation, so they would come out outside as well, at the cost of one more request. The backlog has an item for a lookup that works without repository admin.
data.connect-a-github-repository#Connect a Gi:
Check the route: the startup event “forge route” for github.com shows plugin=github and available=true. Without it, add the entry (see “Add a second forge”):
plugins: github: path: /plugins/github/plugin.wasm authScheme: bearer hosts: - host: github.com apiUrl: https://api.github.com Create a fine-grained personal access token for an account with write access, restricted to the project’s repositories (“Only select repositories”), with the repository permissions Pull requests read/write, Issues read/write, Contents read/write (Git clone and push) and Metadata read. A classic token needs repo. list-feedback reads each reviewer’s repository permission (GET .../collaborators/{username}/permission), which needs the account’s write access.
Store it in a Secret in the instance namespace (sandbox.instanceNamespace), for example kubectl -n dark-factory create secret generic github-token --from-file=token=.
Settings → Credentials → “New credential reference”: a name, Secret name github-token, key token.
Projects → “New project”: repository URL https://github.com//.git and that credential as forge credential. The hint below the repository URL reads “Served by the GitHub integration; pull requests and issues use it.”
No egress rule for github.com is needed. The sandbox clones and pushes through the gateway’s Git proxy, which sends agent.gitUsername and the token upstream; API calls come from the control plane.
data.forge-routing#Forge routing:
Each forge call is routed by the host of the project’s repo_url, normalized like hosts (lowercase, port 443 dropped). Matching is exact: www.example.org, example.org and example.org:3000 are three hosts. A claimed host goes to the plugin claiming it, any other host to the default plugin. A plugin that did not load keeps its hosts: its projects get a config error naming the plugin and never fall through to the default, because their credential is meant for that forge.
flowchart TD H["host of repo_url (normalized)"] --> C{"listed in hosts?"} C -- yes --> CL{"claiming plugin loaded?"} CL -- yes --> R1["claiming plugin, base-url = apiUrl"] CL -- no --> E1["config error: plugin did not load"] C -- no --> D{"default plugin configured?"} D -- no --> E2["config error: no forge plugin serves host"] D -- yes --> DL{"default plugin loaded?"} DL -- yes --> R2["default plugin, base-url = scheme://authority of repo_url"] DL -- no --> E1 With more than one plugin, give every entry hosts: a default plugin also receives projects of forges nobody configured (for example gitlab.com sent to Forgejo) and fails with upstream 401/404. Without a default such projects get a clear config error.
data.forgejo-token-scopes#Forgejo token scope: The bot account’s token needs write:repository (create and update pull requests, read branches), write:issue (comments on issues and pull requests) and read:user (list-feedback reads the token’s own account to label its comments bot; Forgejo 15 answers 403 without this scope). Read-only use needs read:repository, read:issue and read:user.
data.github#GitHub: The github plugin serves github.com and GitHub Enterprise Server. Its settings, draft modes and error mapping: plugins/github/README.md. The Helm chart’s default values route github.com to it.
data.refused-requests#Refused requests: A forge answer 401 or 403 becomes the error unauthorized. Only a 403 on the role lookup is turned into outside (see above); a 401 there is an invalid credential and fails the call. Its message starts with the failed request (GET /api/v1/repos/o/r/pulls/7/reviews: token does not have required scope) followed by the forge’s own message. The agent sees it as a tool error (“the forge refused the request (…)”) and is told to ask a human to check the bot account’s access and the project’s forge credential. A missing scope and a missing repository permission look alike; the request and the forge’s message tell which endpoint failed.
data.startup#Startup:
Without a plugins section (or with an empty one) serve uses one entry forgejo with path /plugins/forgejo/plugin.wasm as the default plugin. As soon as plugins has an entry, there is no implicit forgejo.
serve builds the routing table from the configuration alone. A configuration error stops startup before any plugin loads (event “control plane server failed”, field error): invalid `plugins` configuration: with one of
host `` is claimed by plugins `` and `` plugins ``, `` have no `hosts`; at most one default plugin is allowed plugin ``: apiUrl `` must use https:// plugin ``: invalid apiUrl (not a URL, or with userinfo, query or fragment; the value is not echoed) plugin ``: invalid host in `hosts[]` (index from 0; the value is not echoed) plugin ``: unknown authScheme `` (use `token` or `bearer`) A webhookSecretFile that is missing, unreadable or empty stops startup the same way: cannot read `plugins..webhookSecretFile` `` or `plugins..webhookSecretFile` `` is empty.
It loads every entry. An entry that fails (component missing or invalid, memoryMib too large, or no pull-requests export: “is not a forge plugin”) is logged at error (“forge plugin not loaded”, fields plugin, path, error) and stays in the table as unavailable.
If no forge plugin loaded, serve exits with no forge plugin loaded: .
Otherwise it logs the table at info: one “forge route” per claimed host (fields host, plugin, available, ordered by host), then “default forge route” (plugin, available) or “no default forge route”.
Each successful load is logged at info (“plugin loaded”) with the fields plugin (name under plugins), path, bytes (component size) and compile_ms (load time: everything after the file read, i.e. import validation, compilation and pre-instantiation; the shared engine is created once before). Use it to see what the plugin costs at startup.
Plugin stderr is logged as event “plugin stderr” with the fields plugin (the name under plugins) and line, at warn for a line that starts with warning: (what the forge plugins write for warnings) and at info otherwise; lines longer than 4 KiB are split.
Per project (database): repo_url (https:////[.git], without userinfo, query or fragment) selects the route and gives the repository; base-url comes from the route (see settings). forge_credential_id references the Kubernetes Secret holding the token. Secrets are read per call and not cached.
data.swap-a-plugin-for-a-host#Swap a plugin f:
Projects store no plugin name, so moving a host needs no data change.
Add the new entry (or change path of the existing one to replace only the component).
Move the host from the old entry’s hosts to the new one. Listing it in both fails startup with host `` is claimed by plugins ….
plugins: forgejo: path: /plugins/forgejo/plugin.wasm hosts: [git.example.org] forgejo-next: path: /plugins/forgejo-next/plugin.wasm hosts: [code.example.org] # moved from `forgejo` Check that the projects’ credentials fit the new plugin’s authScheme.
Restart serve; the “forge route” event for the host shows the new plugin. To roll back, move the host back.
data.troubleshoot-an-unroutable-project#Troub:
Read the error of the failed forge call (plugin configuration error: …):
no forge plugin serves host `` : no entry claims the host and there is no default plugin, or the host is not valid. Compare the host with the “forge route” events (port and www. count) and add it to the right entry’s hosts. forge plugin `` serving host `` did not load: find the startup event “forge plugin not loaded” with that plugin; its path and error name the cause. Fix it and restart. invalid repository URL: repo_url is not https:////[.git], or it has userinfo, a query or a fragment. The URL is not echoed: it may carry credentials. repository URL for host `` is not HTTPS: repo_url uses http://; use https://. the project has no forge credential: set the project’s forge credential. Open the project’s edit form. The hint below the repository URL names the routing result:
“Served by the integration; pull requests and issues use it.” “The integration claims this host but is not loaded: …” “The default integration is not loaded: …” “No forge integration applies: …” The project list shows the generic Git icon for a project no loaded integration serves (and for a project without a forge credential).
An upstream 401 or 404 instead of a config error usually means the project went to the default plugin. Check the “forge route” and “default forge route” events and add the host to the entry of its forge.
data.use-title-prefix-drafts#Use title-prefix:
The default draft-mode: native creates GitHub’s native draft pull requests, which also exist in private repositories on GitHub Free.
Pick the mode. Use title-prefix when a repository or GitHub Enterprise Server instance rejects native drafts (creating a draft fails with invalid-input naming draft-mode: title-prefix), or for a WIP: marker in the title consistent with Forgejo. auto creates native drafts where possible and falls back to the title prefix elsewhere, at the cost of one failed request per draft and a warning (event “plugin stderr”, plugin=github, level warn).
Set it in the entry’s settings (chart: plugins.github.settings):
plugins: github: # path, authScheme, hosts unchanged settings: draft-mode: title-prefix # or auto Restart serve. Open drafts keep working: reading recognizes the title prefix and the native flag.

data:
With forge webhooks, a task wakes up when someone reviews its pull request, mentions the bot account, merges or closes the pull request, or when CI fails on its branch. Without them, the task waits until someone writes in the web UI.
Forge event Effect on the task Review submitted (approve, request changes, comment) wakes the task, subject to the wake setting Comment that mentions the bot account (@factory-bot) on the pull request or on the linked issue wakes the task, subject to the wake setting CI failed on factory/task/ wakes the task Pull request closed without merge wakes the task Pull request merged the task becomes completed and its run stops; its volume is deleted at the next hourly check, whatever volumes.retainAfterCloseSeconds says Each accepted event queues one message (reason webhook) on its task: logins, verdicts, check names, numbers and URLs, never review or comment text. The agent reads the feedback with read_pull_request_feedback. Messages that arrive while the agent works wait for the end of its turn, so a burst of events wakes the task once. A task in in_review whose pull request is still open goes back to work and its pull request becomes a draft again; a closed pull request stays as it is. Tasks in completed, cancelled or failed are not woken. The message for a review or a mention also tells the agent to pass the next_since of its last read as since, so it reads only what is new (Review feedback).
sequenceDiagram participant F as Forge participant CP as Control plane participant P as Forge plugin participant DB as Database participant O as Outbox F->>CP: POST /webhooks/ CP->>P: handle-webhook (headers, body) P->>CP: verify signature (HMAC-SHA256) P-->>CP: normalized events CP->>CP: repository match, routing, bot and wake filters alt pull request merged CP->>DB: task completed, active run stopped else review, mention, CI failure, close CP->>DB: queue message (reason webhook) DB->>O: mark-draft job if the task left in_review O->>F: pull request back to draft end CP-->>F: 202 Reviews and comments written by the bot account itself are ignored. Merged, closed and CI events apply whoever triggered them. Reviews, closes and CI runs of pull requests from a fork are ignored, even if the fork’s branch is named factory/task/.
data.choose-who-wakes-tasks#Choose who wakes:
Projects → edit a project → General → Wake tasks on reviews and mentions decides whose reviews and mentions wake the project’s tasks:
Option Reviews and mentions from Nobody nobody; merged, closed and CI events still apply Members with write access (default) accounts with write access or more to the repository Anyone every account except the bot With Members with write access, the control plane asks the forge for the author’s permission on each review or mention. Changes are written to the audit log.
On Forgejo the permission lookup needs a bot account that is repository admin. When the forge refuses it, the author counts as not a member: the event is accepted but does not wake the task, and the log has the plugin’s warning “cannot read the repository permission of …” (event “plugin stderr”). Make the bot account repository admin, or choose Anyone (Bot account access).
data.redeliver-a-failed-delivery#Redeliver a:
Forgejo and GitHub record a delivery answered with 5xx as failed and do not retry it. A lost merge event leaves the task in in_review; a lost review or mention does not wake it.
Forgejo: the webhook’s settings page → Recent deliveries → open the delivery → Replay. GitHub: the webhook’s Recent Deliveries tab → open the delivery → Redeliver, or the REST endpoint POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/hooks/{hook_id}/deliveries/{delivery_id}/attempts. Redelivering is safe: a merge that was already applied does nothing, and a duplicate review adds one more message.
data.register-the-webhook-in-forgejo#Register:
Register it once for all repositories of an organisation (Organisation → Settings → Webhooks) or of the whole instance (Site administration → Integrations → Webhooks → System webhooks). A repository webhook (Repository → Settings → Webhooks) works as well. Choose Add webhook → Forgejo:
Field Value Target URL https://factory.example.org/webhooks/forgejo HTTP method POST POST content type application/json Secret the value from the Secret Trigger on Custom events… Issue events Comments Pull request events Modification, Comments, Reviews Action Run events Failure Active on Forgejo sends no webhook for commit statuses set by an external CI; only failed Forgejo Actions runs wake a task.
Forgejo only delivers to external addresses by default. If the control plane resolves to a private address (for example a cluster-internal name), allow it in Forgejo’s app.ini:
[webhook] ALLOWED_HOST_LIST = factory.example.org
data.register-the-webhook-in-github#Register:
Register it on the organisation (Settings → Webhooks) or on each repository (Settings → Webhooks), with the secret stored under the key of the github plugin (plugins.github.webhookSecret):
Field Value Payload URL https://factory.example.org/webhooks/github Content type application/json Secret the value from the Secret Events Let me select individual events: Check suites, Issue comments, Pull requests, Pull request reviews, Statuses Active on GitHub sends a ping after saving; the control plane answers 202 and ignores it.
data.set-the-webhook-secret#Set the webhook s:
One secret per plugin signs all its deliveries (HMAC-SHA256). Every repository the plugin serves shares it; an event only reaches projects whose repository URL matches the event’s repository.
Create the Secret in the instance namespace:
kubectl -n dark-factory create secret generic forge-webhooks \ --from-literal=forgejo="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" Reference it in the Helm values and run helm upgrade:
plugins: forgejo: webhookSecret: name: forge-webhooks key: forgejo The chart mounts the key read-only at /var/run/dark-factory/webhooks/forgejo/secret and sets plugins.forgejo.webhookSecretFile in the instance configuration. The control plane reads the file once at startup; a missing or empty file stops it (Startup).
Check the endpoint. Without a valid signature it answers 401; 404 means the plugin has no secret or is not loaded:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X POST https://factory.example.org/webhooks/forgejo The endpoint POST /webhooks/ is served on the web UI’s host without login. Bodies over 1 MiB are refused with 413. Rotating the secret means changing it in the Secret and in the forge, then restarting the control plane (kubectl -n dark-factory rollout restart deployment/-control-plane).
data.troubleshooting#Troubleshooting:
The metric df.webhook.requests (Prometheus: df_webhook_requests_total) counts requests by plugin and outcome (Telemetry). Requests for a plugin that is not loaded are counted as plugin="unknown"; a loaded plugin keeps its name.
Outcome Cause not_found Wrong plugin name in the URL, the plugin did not load, it exports no webhook interface, or it has no webhookSecret. unauthorized The secret in the forge differs from the Secret, or the request carries no signature (GitHub: only X-Hub-Signature-256 counts). invalid The plugin could not parse the payload: content type is not JSON, or the event header is missing. too_large Body over 1 MiB. error Storing the events or a forge lookup failed; the control plane logs a warning. Neither forge redelivers on its own: redeliver it once the cause is fixed. accepted but the task does not wake See the debug log below. Accepted events that do not wake a task are logged at debug. Raise the level of these modules:
controlPlane: logLevel: info,dark_factory::forge=debug,df_agent_channel::webhooks=debug,df_db::webhooks=debug Debug message Cause webhook repository matches no project No project has this repository URL (compared by host, owner and name). webhook event names no factory task The pull request’s or CI run’s branch is not factory/task/. webhook event matches no task No task of the project has this key or pull request, or no unfinished task is linked to the commented issue. webhook event dropped The author is the bot account (reason="bot"), or a comment does not mention the bot account (reason="no mention"). webhook author below the wake policy The wake setting is Nobody, or the author has no write access (or the forge refused the permission lookup, see above) and the wake setting is Members with write access. webhook event of a finished task dropped The task is completed, cancelled or failed. webhook signature not verified As outcome unauthorized.

data:
Dark Factory notifies external systems when a task’s volume or a run’s sandbox is created or destroyed. Each event is an HTTP POST with a JSON body, signed with the instance’s Ed25519 key in the Standard Webhooks v1a scheme. Delivery is at least once, retried for 24 hours, and never delays a run.
Typical receivers: wake a GPU or build node before a sandbox needs it, track sandbox minutes per project, or feed an audit log.
data.address-filter#Address filter:
Project subscriptions are configured by project admins in the UI, so their targets are restricted:
The URL must be https://. An IP literal in the URL must be public; this is checked on save and before each attempt. Before each attempt the host is resolved, and the attempt is refused (address refused: …) if any resolved address is loopback, private (RFC 1918), CGNAT (100.64.0.0/10), link-local (including 169.254.169.254), unique-local (fc00::/7), unspecified, broadcast or documentation, or an IPv4-mapped IPv6 form of these. The checked address is the one connected to, so DNS rebinding does not get around it. Redirects are not followed, and no proxy from the environment is used. Limits: the filter knows only these well-known ranges. It does not know a cluster’s own public address ranges (pod or Service CIDRs outside the private ranges) or internal services reachable on public addresses. To restrict the control plane further, add an egress NetworkPolicy. The chart’s control plane NetworkPolicy restricts ingress only. An egress policy must still allow everything else the control plane talks to (DNS, PostgreSQL, the Kubernetes API, the OIDC provider, forges, the gateway, instance receivers). Sketch:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: dark-factory-control-plane-egress namespace: dark-factory spec: podSelector: matchLabels: app.kubernetes.io/instance: dark-factory app.kubernetes.io/component: control-plane policyTypes: [Egress] egress: # ... rules for DNS, PostgreSQL, the Kubernetes API, the OIDC provider, the gateway ... - to: - ipBlock: cidr: 0.0.0.0/0 except: [203.0.113.0/24] # internal ranges the address filter does not know ports: - {protocol: TCP, port: 443} Instance subscriptions are trusted configuration and bypass the filter.
For development, a dev-tools build accepts --unrestricted-project-subscriptions, which lifts the restrictions for project subscriptions (development.md). Release builds don’t have the flag.
data.delivery#Delivery:
Request: POST with the envelope as body and these headers:
Header Value content-type application/json webhook-id event ID (evt_…), the same on every attempt webhook-timestamp Unix seconds of this attempt webhook-signature v1a, over .. Success: any 2xx within 10 s. Redirects are not followed and count as failure. Retries: after attempt n fails, the next one follows after min(30 s · 2^(n−1), 1 h). An attempt due more than 24 h after the event is not sent; the delivery is given up. At least once: a control plane restart during a request sends the event again. Deduplicate by webhook-id. No ordering: events can arrive in any order, also for the same run. Order by timestamp or match by data.run.id. Independent receivers: each subscription has its own retries; a dead receiver does not hold back others. No effect on runs: a failing or slow receiver never delays provisioning, teardown or any state change. At most 8 requests are in flight per instance. sequenceDiagram participant S as Scheduler / agent channel participant DB as PostgreSQL participant D as Outbox dispatcher (leader) participant R as Receiver S->>DB: BEGIN, state change (for example mark_started) S->>DB: INSERT lifecycle_events (envelope, built once) S->>DB: INSERT outbox job per matching subscription S->>DB: COMMIT, NOTIFY outbox DB-->>D: NOTIFY outbox (fallback: 5 s poll) D->>DB: claim due jobs (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED), set lease; give up jobs older than 24 h D->>D: project subscription: resolve host, refuse internal addresses D->>D: sign id.timestamp.body D->>R: POST envelope with webhook-* headers (10 s timeout) alt 2xx R-->>D: 2xx D->>DB: job done, subscription last status else error, timeout, non-2xx or refused address D->>DB: next attempt after backoff, last error end An event is recorded in the same transaction as the state change: a rolled-back change sends nothing, a committed one is delivered even if the control plane restarts first.
data.event-catalog#Event catalog:
Every event has the same envelope:
Field Content id evt_ + UUIDv7; equals the webhook-id header type event type, see below timestamp RFC 3339 time of the state change (not of the delivery attempt) data.project id, key, repo_url data.task id, key data.persona id, name data.run id, number; missing for volume.destroyed Values are a snapshot at the time of the event: a later rename does not change events already recorded.
Type When Extra fields in data sandbox.provisioning The scheduler starts provisioning a run, before volume and sandbox are created. Once per run. none volume.provisioned The task volume (task-) was created for the first time. Once per task; again after the volume was deleted. Carries the run that created it. none sandbox.provisioned The provider reports the run’s pod as running. Does not wait for the agent to connect. none sandbox.provisioning_failed Creating the volume or the sandbox failed. No sandbox.destroyed follows for the run. error (text) sandbox.destroyed A run whose provisioning began ended and its teardown was issued. outcome, started_at (when the pod came up, null if it never did), ended_at volume.destroyed The task volume was deleted. reason: retention or reset outcome is one of completed, end_turn, blocked, limit_reached, rate_limited, cancelled, failed, connect_timeout, sandbox_lost. A run cancelled while still provisioning gets cancelled with started_at: null.
Where each event fires in a run: the sequence diagram in design/agent-run.md §6.0.
Example delivery (sandbox.provisioned, captured from the e2e suite; the body is sent compact, formatted here):
POST /hook HTTP/1.1 content-type: application/json webhook-id: evt_01a1a35b-6980-74e1-a69a-5ff710ca948d webhook-timestamp: 1793742039 webhook-signature: v1a,qx0/bYj8Yk3QuiiRYr4LnjrJI9RdOU6TMWz/5ZS52HZj8MBsL2mAeOUIuCcz4kRAmg6ixJxF4lICOBwqj5SFBA== { "id": "evt_01a1a35b-6980-74e1-a69a-5ff710ca948d", "data": { "run": {"id": "01a1a35b-5603-70f9-a97d-40ff01958ead", "number": 1}, "task": {"id": "01a1a35b-55f9-7464-b9de-d50e9dab11f8", "key": "DF-1"}, "persona": {"id": "01a1a35b-23f3-75a5-8fe4-4a97a86da9bf", "name": "e2e"}, "project": { "id": "01a1a35b-23fc-7048-b801-f2b4602bc70b", "key": "DF", "repo_url": "http://forgejo-http.forgejo.svc:3000/factory/demo" } }, "type": "sandbox.provisioned", "timestamp": "2026-11-03T21:40:39.422Z" }
data.how-to-add-a-project-subscription-and-ve:
Get the role admin (Authentication; Keycloak: client role, Dex: group). Open Projects, click the edit icon of the project and choose the tab Lifecycle events, then New subscription. The form opens inside the tab. Enter the receiver URL (https://, public host), check the event types (none: all) and click Create subscription or press Enter in the URL field. An invalid URL keeps the form open with an error at the field. Copy the public key whpk_… from the tab into the receiver’s configuration. In the receiver, verify every delivery (Verifying signatures) and drop duplicates by webhook-id. Start a task in the project. Its first run sends sandbox.provisioning, volume.provisioned and sandbox.provisioned. The tab then shows the last attempt, for example HTTP 204. Subscriptions save on their own: creating, editing and deleting take effect at once, “Save project” does not apply to them, and cancelling the project dialog keeps them. The pencil icon of a row edits it in place. One form is open at a time: opening another discards the unsaved values of the first. The trash icon asks “Delete this subscription? Deliveries to it stop at once.” in the row; only Delete removes the subscription.
A failing receiver shows the error or status of its last attempt in the tab (address refused: …, timed out, connection failed: …, HTTP 503). Delivery is retried in the background (Delivery).
data.how-to-wake-a-node-before-a-sandbox-star:
Goal: a node that is normally off (a GPU box on the LAN, a spot VM) boots when a run needs it and shuts down when no run uses it.
Use an instance subscription. A project subscription refuses private LAN addresses, so a wake-on-LAN bridge in the cluster or on the LAN must be an instance receiver:
lifecycleEvents: subscriptions: - url: http://wol-bridge.infra.svc:8080/events events: [sandbox.provisioning, sandbox.provisioning_failed, sandbox.destroyed] Wake on sandbox.provisioning. The scheduler emits it when it picks the run, before it creates the volume and the sandbox; a run waiting in the queue emits nothing yet. Dark Factory does not wait for the receiver: the sandbox pod stays Pending until the node joins and can take it. The node must be ready within runs.connectTimeoutSeconds (default 600 s), which counts from run creation. Otherwise the run ends with connect_timeout.
Shut down by matching per run. Every sandbox.provisioning is followed by exactly one sandbox.provisioning_failed or sandbox.destroyed with the same data.run.id. Keep the set of open run IDs: add on sandbox.provisioning, remove on either closing event. Delivery order is not guaranteed, so remember closed run IDs for a while and ignore a late sandbox.provisioning for one of them. Shut the node down after the set has been empty for a grace period.
Make each step idempotent: the same event can arrive twice (same webhook-id).
To target only some projects, filter on data.project.key in the receiver.
data.key-rotation#Key rotation: The key is stable: the chart creates it with cert-manager rotationPolicy: Never, and certificate renewal keeps it. Rotation is manual: delete the key Secret, restart the control plane, give receivers the new public key (steps: chart README, “Lifecycle event signing key”). Until a receiver has the new key, its verification fails; the deliveries are retried for 24 h, so a receiver that updates within that window and answers non-2xx meanwhile loses nothing. Receivers can fetch GET /lifecycle-events/public-key to automate the update.
data.subscriptions#Subscriptions:
Instance subscription Project subscription Receives events of every project events of one project Managed in control plane configuration (Helm lifecycleEvents.subscriptions), restart to apply UI: Projects → edit a project → tab “Lifecycle events”; needs the role admin, other users do not see the tab URL http:// or https://, any address including cluster-internal services https:// only; the host must resolve to public addresses (Address filter); no username or password in the URL (it is written to the audit log) Delivery status control plane logs last attempt (time, HTTP status or error) in the tab “Lifecycle events” Each subscription lists the event types it receives. An empty list means all types, including types added later.
The instance public key is served without authentication at GET /lifecycle-events/public-key (text/plain, whpk_) and shown at the top of every project’s tab “Lifecycle events”. Without a signing key the feature is off: nothing is recorded, the endpoint returns 404 and the tab says so (existing subscriptions stay listed).
Instance subscriptions in the Helm values (reference: chart README, lifecycleEvents.*):
lifecycleEvents: subscriptions: - url: http://audit.observability.svc:8080/events events: [sandbox.destroyed] Outside the chart, the control plane config.yaml takes the same list plus the key path:
lifecycleEvents: signingKeyFile: /run/secrets/lifecycle-events/tls.key # Ed25519, PEM PKCS#8 subscriptions: [] # as above With subscriptions configured but no signingKeyFile, the control plane refuses to start.
data.verifying-signatures#Verifying signature:
Verify every delivery with the instance public key before trusting the body. Reject attempts whose webhook-timestamp is more than a few minutes off to limit replays; retries carry a fresh timestamp. webhook-signature may hold several space-separated signatures; accept the request if one verifies.
Python (cryptography):
import base64 import json import time from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidSignature from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.ed25519 import Ed25519PublicKey TOLERANCE_SECONDS = 300 def verify(public_key: str, headers: dict[str, str], body: bytes) -> dict: """Returns the event if the delivery is signed by `public_key` (`whpk_…`), else raises.""" key = Ed25519PublicKey.from_public_bytes(base64.b64decode(public_key.removeprefix("whpk_"))) msg_id = headers["webhook-id"] timestamp = headers["webhook-timestamp"] if abs(time.time() - int(timestamp)) > TOLERANCE_SECONDS: raise ValueError("webhook-timestamp outside the tolerance") message = f"{msg_id}.{timestamp}.".encode() + body for signature in headers["webhook-signature"].split(" "): version, _, value = signature.partition(",") if version != "v1a": continue try: key.verify(base64.b64decode(value), message) except InvalidSignature: continue return json.loads(body) raise ValueError("no valid signature") Go (standard library):
package webhook import ( "crypto/ed25519" "encoding/base64" "errors" "net/http" "strconv" "strings" "time" ) const tolerance = 5 * time.Minute // Verify returns nil if the delivery is signed by publicKey (`whpk_…`). func Verify(publicKey string, header http.Header, body []byte) error { key, err := base64.StdEncoding.DecodeString(strings.TrimPrefix(publicKey, "whpk_")) if err != nil || len(key) != ed25519.PublicKeySize { return errors.New("invalid public key") } id, timestamp := header.Get("webhook-id"), header.Get("webhook-timestamp") seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(timestamp, 10, 64) if err != nil { return errors.New("invalid webhook-timestamp") } if age := time.Since(time.Unix(seconds, 0)); age > tolerance || age < -tolerance { return errors.New("webhook-timestamp outside the tolerance") } message := append([]byte(id+"."+timestamp+"."), body...) for _, signature := range strings.Fields(header.Get("webhook-signature")) { version, value, ok := strings.Cut(signature, ",") if !ok || version != "v1a" { continue } raw, err := base64.StdEncoding.DecodeString(value) if err == nil && ed25519.Verify(ed25519.PublicKey(key), message, raw) { return nil } } return errors.New("no valid signature") } Verify against the raw request body, before any JSON parsing or re-encoding.

data: Logging: log format and levels of all components, and the sandbox session events. Telemetry: OpenTelemetry metrics and traces of the control plane and the gateway.
